title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Neuroimaging — October 2026

studies.title: Most children who feel lonely at 10 are still lonely at 14
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: huge pre-existing cohort, prospective design and a genuinely sobering headline number; limited by the fact that the brain findings are the weakest part.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers screened 347 environmental exposures, 61 health indicators and 558 MRI measures (gray matter volume, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity) in 9,602 children from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, all aged 9–10 at baseline, and tracked loneliness reports to age 14. Of the 12% who reported loneliness at baseline, 71.6% reported it again over the next three years. The strongest correlates were not neural but domestic: parental psychopathology, developmental history and family income, with general mental health the single largest health effect; MRI features that discriminated lonely from non-lonely children clustered in socioemotional processing systems.
studies.why_it_matters: Childhood loneliness is usually framed as a passing phase, and this is the largest prospective test of that assumption — it suggests loneliness at 10 is a fairly durable state, and that the measurable risk factors sit in the family and neighborhood rather than in the scanner.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the number — seven in ten lonely 10-year-olds are still lonely three years later. Open on the scale of the screen (nearly a thousand variables, nearly 10,000 children) and the slightly deflating result that the brain scans added less than the household income question did. Worth calling Tsz Yeung Wong at the Education University of Hong Kong, and Ruben Gur's group at Penn for the imaging side.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for an education or policy outlet on whether "loneliness screening" in schools is a good idea at all — this dataset identifies persistent loneliness but offers no validated intervention, and the risk factors it flags (parental mental illness, poverty) are ones schools can detect without asking children to self-label.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; self-reported (and in part caregiver-reported) outcomes; the neuroimaging component is a discriminant-analysis classification rather than a tested mechanism; ABCD is US-based and 55% White, so generalization is limited.

studies.title: Brain scans during a failed night's sleep show what insomnia actually looks like
studies.ns_score_reason: scanning people while they try and fail to fall asleep is a vivid, highly relatable first; badly limited by 11 patients.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Eleven people with insomnia disorder and 17 good sleepers underwent arterial spin labelling MRI — which measures blood flow without a tracer — twice in the same night: once awake at their habitual bedtime, and once during an actual sleep attempt, with polysomnography confirming sleep state. People with insomnia showed higher relative perfusion in posterior sensory, affective and self-referential regions, and lower perfusion in frontal cortex and basal ganglia. Strikingly, insomnia participants who did manage to fall asleep showed *lower* frontal and basal ganglia perfusion than those who stayed awake — the opposite of the pattern in controls.
studies.why_it_matters: It is direct physiological evidence for the long-argued "hyperarousal" account of insomnia, and the inverted sleep-state pattern hints that the brain's switch into sleep is wired differently in insomnia rather than simply running late. With 28 people total, though, this is a proof-of-concept that opens a line of enquiry rather than settling one.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the experimental scene — someone lying in an MRI scanner at their usual bedtime, instructed to try to sleep, while the machine tracks blood flowing to the parts of their brain that will not stop thinking about themselves. The hook is the reversal: when insomniacs do fall asleep, their frontal control regions go quieter than when they are awake, while good sleepers' go busier. Call Daniel B. Kay at Brigham Young University, and Lars Michels in Zurich.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist piece for a clinical or sleep-medicine readership on whether nighttime imaging can finally separate "paradoxical insomnia" — people who sleep by polysomnography but experience wakefulness — from objective short sleep, and what that would mean for how insomnia is classified.
studies.caveats: Very small N (11 vs 17); single-center; relative rather than absolute perfusion maps; exploratory cluster-corrected voxelwise analysis with a lenient voxel threshold; cross-sectional.

studies.title: Lab experiments missed a brain network that decides where you look
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat demonstration that decades of tidy attention experiments overlooked something, with a successful replication built in; limited by a modest sample and correlational pattern analysis.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Participants watched a movie in an fMRI scanner while their eye fixations were tracked. Comparing how fixation patterns and brain activation patterns shifted between scenes reproduced the classic dorsal and ventral attention networks — but the differences *between individuals* in where they chose to look were mirrored instead by activity in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, regions not previously implicated in human eye-movement control. The effect was strongest for scenes containing faces.
studies.why_it_matters: Attention research has been built on abstract stimuli and explicit instructions, and this suggests that design systematically hid the machinery behind free, socially motivated gaze choices — the "where shall I look" decisions that make up almost all real-world looking.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the methodological twist: the same study both replicates the textbook attention networks and shows they are not what makes your gaze differ from the person next to you in the cinema. Open on two people watching the same scene and looking at completely different things. Call Nico Marek or Stefan Pollmann at Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg.
studies.wider_angle: A trend feature for a neuroscience or technology outlet on the broader shift to "naturalistic neuroimaging" — movies, conversations, video games in the scanner — and what established findings are now being quietly revised as a result.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract and likely small; correlational representational-similarity approach cannot establish that the orbitofrontal–anterior temporal network causes gaze decisions; single-center; one movie stimulus.

studies.title: Impulsive suicidal thoughts leave a different mark on the brain than planned ones
studies.ns_score_reason: resolves a real puzzle in the ENIGMA literature with a decent clinical sample; limited by a single-item measure of ideation subtype.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Large consortium studies had found reduced thalamus and pallidum volumes in people who had attempted suicide, but nothing comparable for suicidal ideation — an awkward gap, since ideation precedes attempt. Analyzing structural MRI from 263 people with major depressive disorder, the authors split ideation into "hot" (affectively driven, unplanned) and "cold" (deliberate, planned) using the MADRS suicide item. Reduced thalamo-pallidal volume was associated with hot ideation only, and survived adjustment for depression severity, history of attempt and dorsolateral prefrontal volume.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the missing brain signature for suicidal thinking was hidden by lumping two very different mental states together, and gives researchers a concrete reason to stop treating ideation as one thing. It is an association in a depressed sample, not a predictive test.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a measurement failure, not a brain discovery: a decade of imaging found nothing for suicidal ideation because "thinking about suicide" was treated as a single variable. Open on the hot/cold distinction — the difference between a sudden overwhelming urge and a slowly assembled plan — and what emotional-reactivity hubs like the thalamus and pallidum are thought to do. Call Armand Chatard at the Université de Poitiers. Avoid any suggestion that a scan could identify risk in an individual.
studies.wider_angle: A measurement-science feature for a psychiatry or health-policy outlet on how much of the field's biomarker disappointment traces back to coarse symptom scales — the suicide item of the MADRS was never designed to carve a phenotype, yet subtype-blind pooling is standard across consortium neuroimaging.
studies.caveats: Observational, cross-sectional; ideation subtype derived from a single rating-scale item; no healthy control comparison; single-site clinical sample of people with MDD, so may not generalize; sensitive subject requiring careful framing.

studies.title: Catatonia may be the ancient freeze response jammed on
studies.ns_score_reason: a strong, testable idea with real explanatory reach, but it is a review-and-synthesis rather than new data.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: The authors systematically cross-referenced human neuroimaging of normal threat-induced freezing against imaging of catatonia across its many causes. Both literatures implicate the same three things: failure of orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex, salience network dysregulation, and a basal ganglia–midbrain motor block. From this they build the "freeze-arrest model of catatonia", with three entry points — overwhelming emotion, toxic-metabolic network disruption, and subcortical short-circuiting — and argue that neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental catatonia is a mechanistically separate category.
studies.why_it_matters: Catatonia is one of psychiatry's strangest and most poorly defined syndromes, and framing akinetic catatonia as a maladaptive version of the freeze-to-tonic-immobility response conserved across vertebrates gives clinicians a mechanistic reason for why the presentations and treatment responses differ so much.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the evolutionary image — the same circuitry that freezes a rabbit in the open may, in humans, lock a person into immobility for days. Open on the clinical picture of akinetic catatonia and the puzzle of why a benzodiazepine can release it within minutes. Call Anthony Chabbouh at the Lebanese University / American University of Beirut and ask what observation would falsify the model.
studies.wider_angle: A history-of-medicine feature for a general-interest magazine on catatonia's disappearance and return — once thought a form of schizophrenia, now recognized across autism, encephalitis, mood disorders and critical illness — and what it says about how diagnostic categories are made and unmade.
studies.caveats: Narrative/critical review, not primary research; no quantitative meta-analysis; the model is explicitly untested; underlying imaging studies of catatonia are mostly small and heterogeneous.

studies.title: Feeling rejected makes you lonely through a specific psychological step — and it looks different in older brains
studies.ns_score_reason: decent sample spanning two age groups and open data, but the headline neural findings are exploratory and the design cannot order the causal chain.
studies.the_study: 249 people — 141 aged 18–34 and 108 aged 60–89 — completed measures of perceived rejection, withdrawal-related threat sensitivity and loneliness, and had structural MRI. Threat sensitivity partially accounted for the link between perceived rejection and loneliness in both age groups, but older adults reported lower average threat sensitivity *and* lower loneliness than the young. Exploratory analyses linked gray matter volume in self-referential and social-perceptual regions (left angular gyrus, precuneus, subparietal sulcus, planum temporale, right superior temporal sulcus) to this pathway, with precuneus and planum temporale effects appearing only in the younger group.
studies.why_it_matters: It pushes against the cliché of lonely old age: here the older adults were less socially threat-sensitive and less lonely than the under-35s, and the brain structure associated with the rejection-to-loneliness route was detectable mainly in the young.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the age inversion — the people reporting most loneliness were the 18-to-34s, not the 60-to-89s — and the proposed mechanism: rejection breeds loneliness by ratcheting up a habit of withdrawal, not directly. Open on an ambiguous social snub and the two ways a 25-year-old and a 70-year-old might read it. Call Lulu Liu at the University of Macau.
studies.wider_angle: A reanalysis-culture story for a research-practice or data-science outlet: this paper is built from an openly shared OSF/OpenNeuro dataset collected for an entirely different purpose ("Goal-Directed Cognition in Older and Younger Adults"). A good peg for a piece on what open neuroimaging archives are actually producing — and the multiple-comparisons hazards that come with them.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional — mediation here cannot establish causal order; neuroimaging analyses explicitly exploratory; all psychological measures self-reported; secondary analysis of an existing dataset; age differences confounded with cohort effects.

studies.title: People who fear punishment are better at waiting for a reward
studies.ns_score_reason: a tidy, surprising behavioral result with a structural and functional correlate; limited by unreported sample size and a statistically delicate mediation.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Combining behavioral measures, voxel-based morphometry and resting-state fMRI, researchers found that punishment sensitivity — the tendency to notice and react to negative outcomes — was *negatively* correlated with delay discounting, meaning more punishment-sensitive people devalued future rewards less. Gray matter volume in left dorsomedial prefrontal cortex tracked punishment sensitivity, as did its resting connectivity with right postcentral gyrus, and that connectivity partially mediated the behavioral link (with a suppressor effect).
studies.why_it_matters: Sensitivity to punishment is usually filed under anxiety-adjacent liabilities, so finding that it travels with greater patience for delayed rewards complicates the standard reward-and-punishment framing of self-control. Modest and correlational, but a genuinely counterintuitive peg.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook writes itself: the trait that makes you flinch at bad outcomes may be the same one that stops you taking the smaller-sooner payoff. Open on the classic choice — £50 now or £80 in a month — and who actually waits. Call Pan Feng or Tingyong Feng at Southwest University, Chongqing, and press on the suppressor effect, which is a sign the model is doing something subtle.
studies.wider_angle: A behavioral-economics feature for a business or psychology outlet on how personality fits into discounting models — pension saving, climate behavior and debt are all framed through impatience, yet this suggests fear of loss, not optimism about the future, may be what buys patience.
studies.caveats: Sample size not stated in the abstract; cross-sectional and correlational; self-reported trait measure of punishment sensitivity; resting-state connectivity–behavior correlations of this kind are known to require large samples for stability; single-center student-aged population likely.

studies.title: Your sense of numbers runs through the part of the brain that moves your body
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean behavior–brain dissociation that bears on the embodied-cognition debate; narrow topic and likely small sample hold it back.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Participants performed parity judgments (odd/even) and magnitude classifications in an fMRI scanner while researchers applied multivariate pattern analysis. Cardinal (how many) and ordinal (what position) number semantics could be decoded across tasks within sensorimotor cortex, implying shared neural substrates. But there was a dissociation: the classic SNARC effect — small numbers answered faster on the left, large on the right — showed up behaviorally only in the implicit parity task, while sensorimotor decoding was strongest in the explicit magnitude task.
studies.why_it_matters: The "mental number line" is usually described as an abstract spatial representation; this points instead to numerical evaluation being functionally coupled to motor preparation, and shows the famous behavioral signature of the number line and its neural correlate do not appear in the same conditions.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the strange, reproducible fact that your left hand is faster for small numbers and your right for large ones, then deliver the twist: the brain signature of that spatial mapping shows up when the effect is behaviorally absent. Good vehicle for explaining embodied cognition to readers who think arithmetic happens in some abstract symbol-processing module. Call Zhiwei Zhang at Guizhou Normal University.
studies.wider_angle: An education-focused piece for a specialist teaching or child-development outlet on finger counting and gesture in early math learning — if number sense is wired into action systems, the pedagogical arguments about whether to discourage finger counting look different.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract; single-center; decoding results are correlational and cannot show sensorimotor cortex is necessary for numerical semantics; the behavior–brain dissociation is itself unexplained and needs replication.

studies.title: For Māori, the brain is sacred — and MRI practice has no rules for that
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely first-of-its-kind look at whose values are built into neuroimaging protocols; three participants means it carries no statistical weight at all.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using a Māori-centred approach, researchers conducted semi-structured interviews (uiuinga) with three Māori men aged 20, 21 and 46 who had previously taken part in an EEG session, co-led by Māori and non-Māori researchers. Reflexive thematic analysis identified needs around relational engagement, culturally grounded communication for shared decision-making, and integration of Māori values to support whānau (family) confidence and agency. A second collective analysis stage involving participants, te reo Māori and tikanga experts fed into co-designing the first draft neuroimaging guidelines for Aotearoa New Zealand.
studies.why_it_matters: In te ao Māori the head, and the roro (brain) in particular, is the most tapu part of the body — yet there are no national guidelines for conducting neuroimaging accordingly. This is a concrete example of how a technology presented as culturally neutral carries assumptions that affect who consents to be scanned, and therefore who is represented in brain datasets.
studies.pitch_angle: Open with the collision: a procedure that routinely involves touching, gelling and electrode-capping the head, performed in a country where the head is the most sacred part of the body, with no agreed protocol. Then the constructive turn — participants, language experts and researchers co-writing guidelines. Call Ebony Komene at the University of Auckland or Hinemoa Elder at Te Whare Wānanga o Awanuiārangi.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a global-health or science-culture outlet on the representativeness crisis in brain imaging: datasets that underpin "the human brain" are overwhelmingly drawn from a narrow slice of humanity, and cultural barriers to participation are a rarely named reason why. Indigenous data sovereignty initiatives in New Zealand, Canada and Australia give it reach.
studies.caveats: Qualitative study with three participants, all male; findings are not generalizable in a statistical sense and are not intended to be; proposed guideline is explicitly described by the authors as an iterative starting point.

studies.title: In gaming disorder, the brain's reward circuit reacts oddly to rewards that have nothing to do with games
studies.ns_score_reason: the intrinsic-reward angle is the interesting bit, but 44 participants and a complex connectivity analysis make it fragile.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: 21 people meeting criteria for internet gaming disorder and 23 recreational gamers viewed intrinsic reward, extrinsic reward, neutral and gaming cues during fMRI. The gaming disorder group responded faster to gaming cues and reported stronger craving, as expected — but also evaluated intrinsic rewards differently and showed excessive striatum–thalamus synchronization (notably left thalamus to right caudate) specifically while processing intrinsic rewards. Under gaming cues, they showed stronger coupling between the default mode network and reward hubs such as the nucleus accumbens–prefrontal pathway.
studies.why_it_matters: Most addiction imaging looks at how the brain responds to the addictive cue itself; the suggestion here is that gaming disorder also distorts how non-gaming intrinsic rewards — curiosity, mastery, enjoyment for its own sake — are processed. That is a different and more interesting claim, if it replicates.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the counterintuitive bit: the differences were not only about games. Open on the recreational-gamer comparison group, which is the study's real strength — these are not gamers versus non-gamers but heavy gamers versus people with impaired control. Call Guang-Heng Dong at Yunnan Normal University, who has spent a decade on this question.
studies.wider_angle: A critical examination for a technology or games-industry outlet of whether "internet gaming disorder" is a coherent diagnosis at all — it sits in the ICD-11 and the DSM-5 research appendix, and the underlying neuroimaging base consists largely of studies with a few dozen participants. Good place to interview sceptics as well as proponents.
studies.caveats: Small N (21 vs 23); cross-sectional, so cannot tell whether altered reward processing precedes or follows heavy gaming; seed-based connectivity with multiple conditions invites false positives; single-center, likely young adult Chinese sample; the proposed "self-efficacy-sensory drive" model is speculative.

studies.title: Depressed people who are sleepy by day lose pleasure in physical things
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific and testable symptom link with objective sleep recording, but the sample is small and the mediation claim outruns the design.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: 22 patients with major depression and daytime sleepiness (Epworth score ≥7) were compared with 45 depressed patients without it, all undergoing resting-state fMRI, polysomnography and symptom scales. The two groups were matched on depression and anxiety severity *and* on objective sleep parameters, yet the sleepy group scored higher specifically on physical anhedonia — not social or anticipatory anhedonia. They also showed reduced connectivity between default mode and frontoparietal networks (ventrolateral prefrontal cortex to posterior cingulate and precuneus) and widely reduced global and local network efficiency; the vlPFC–PCC link statistically mediated the sleepiness–anhedonia association.
studies.why_it_matters: Daytime sleepiness in depression is usually explained away as poor sleep, but here the polysomnography was equivalent between groups — suggesting sleepiness is tracking something about brain network organization and the capacity to enjoy physical sensation, rather than simply sleep quantity.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the clinical puzzle: two patients with identical depression scores and identical sleep studies, one of whom cannot stay awake through the afternoon and has stopped enjoying food, warmth and touch. The hook is the dissociation between objective sleep and subjective sleepiness. Call Dao-Min Zhu at Anhui Mental Health Center and ask whether the effect survives in a larger sample.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a clinical or neurology-focused outlet on anhedonia as a measurement problem — physical, social and anticipatory pleasure are routinely bundled into one depression item, and studies like this suggest they come apart and point to different circuits.
studies.caveats: Small N (22 vs 45) and unbalanced groups; cross-sectional, so mediation analysis cannot establish a causal sequence; patients were medicated (covariate-adjusted only); anhedonia and sleepiness both self-reported; single-center.

citation_table.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- *Loneliness keeps coming back as a neuro-target, and keeps resisting.* The previous digest's transdiagnostic marker — reduced dorsomedial prefrontal connectivity tracking social dysfunction across schizophrenia, depression and Alzheimer's ("A brain marker for loneliness shows up across depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's", PMID 42044556) — now sits alongside two further loneliness papers: "Most children who feel lonely at 10 are still lonely at 14" (PMID 42186177) and "Feeling rejected makes you lonely through a specific psychological step" (PMID 42091836). Both locate the action in self-referential and social-perceptual cortex, consistent with the dmPFC result.
- *Behavioral addiction imaging continues to drift off the dopamine-reward script.* "In gaming disorder, the brain's reward circuit reacts oddly to rewards that have nothing to do with games" (PMID 42335494) extends last run's two entries from the same literature — the cerebellum-as-top-discriminator classifier (PMID 42727812, same senior author, Guang-Heng Dong) and the digital-addiction meta-analysis implicating serotonergic and GABAergic systems rather than dopamine (PMID 42190596).
- *Symptom lumping is the recurring explanation for null imaging results.* "Impulsive suicidal thoughts leave a different mark on the brain than planned ones" (PMID 42710718) and "Depressed people who are sleepy by day lose pleasure in physical things" (PMID 42746369) both find signal only after splitting a standard symptom construct — exactly the move that separated diminished motivation from diminished expressivity in last run's schizophrenia covariance study (PMID 42176687).
- *Small-N, single-center positives still dominate the softer end.* The insomnia perfusion study (11 vs 17, PMID 42458639), the gaming-disorder scan (21 vs 23, PMID 42335494) and the depression-sleepiness study (22 vs 45, PMID 42746369) sit in the same fragility bracket as last run's trust game (N=31, PMID 42341477) and NODDI sleep apnea groups (n≈24, PMID 42687385).

**Advances**
- Sleep imaging moves from daytime structure to the night itself: last run's NODDI grey-matter study of obstructive sleep apnea (PMID 42687385) scanned awake patients, whereas "Brain scans during a failed night's sleep show what insomnia actually looks like" (PMID 42458639) images people mid-attempt at sleep with polysomnography confirming state — a genuine methodological step, on a much smaller sample.
- Last run's heritage-language work used a naturalistic story stimulus to escape the lab paradigm (PMID 42667920); "Lab experiments missed a brain network that decides where you look" (PMID 42772940) pushes that further by showing a free-viewing movie design recovers the textbook attention networks *and* reveals an orbitofrontal–anterior temporal system that instructed-cue experiments never saw.

**Counterpoints**
- The sharpest tension in the two digests is about how much the scanner adds. Last run's dmPFC loneliness marker (PMID 42044556) was framed as a transdiagnostic neural correlate worth chasing; this run's ABCD screen of 558 MRI measures against 347 exposures (PMID 42186177) finds parental psychopathology and family income outperform anything in the imaging data. Read together, they ask whether the loneliness biomarker literature is measuring the household.
- Age framing also flips: nothing in the previous digest contradicted the standard lonely-old-age picture, but PMID 42091836 reports lower threat sensitivity *and* lower loneliness in the 60–89 group than the 18–34 group.

**New themes**
- *Whose values are in the protocol.* "For Māori, the brain is sacred — and MRI practice has no rules for that" (PMID 42503436) reframes last run's "imaging leaving the undergraduate pool" thread (coal miners, organ donors, bilingual children) as a question about consent, tapu and data sovereignty rather than recruitment reach.
- *Evolutionary and embodied explanations.* The freeze-arrest model of catatonia (PMID 42815707), numerical semantics decoded in sensorimotor cortex (PMID 42764054) and punishment sensitivity predicting patience (PMID 42800541) are all mechanism-first arguments with no counterpart in the previous batch.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch report that a neural signal appears only once a standard symptom label is cut in half — reduced thalamo-pallidal volume tracks "hot" unplanned suicidal ideation but not planned ideation (PMID 42710718); daytime sleepiness in depression maps onto physical anhedonia specifically, not social or anticipatory (PMID 42746369); gaming disorder shows striatal–thalamic abnormality while processing intrinsic rewards rather than game cues (PMID 42335494); and individual differences in free gaze are carried by orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, invisible to the group-level attention networks that instructed tasks produce (PMID 42772940). The counterweight is the ABCD loneliness screen (PMID 42186177), where 558 imaging measures were beaten by the family-income question — a reminder that splitting phenotypes can also simply reveal there was never much there.

**Why pitch this now:** Psychiatric neuroimaging has spent a decade explaining its null results by appealing to sample size, and these papers advance a cheaper and more awkward explanation — that the rating-scale items used to define the phenotype, in one case a single MADRS line, were never built to carve a brain-relevant category.

**Angle:** A reported piece on where psychiatric phenotypes actually come from: who wrote the scale items that consortium studies now pool millions of scans against, what happens when researchers split them, and whether the field's biomarker disappointment is a measurement problem wearing a biology costume. For readers who follow psychiatry and research methods and have already heard the "brain imaging doesn't replicate" story.

**Potential headlines:**
- Brain signals for depression and suicidal thinking appear only when the symptom is split in two
- The problem with psychiatric brain scans may be the questionnaire, not the scanner
- Your diagnosis rests on symptom checklists that the brain does not recognize

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the hot/cold suicidal ideation result and the anhedonia split give the measurement argument two concrete clinical scenes, which is what this section needs to carry an abstract methods story.
- **The Transmitter** — built for exactly this audience of neuroscientists arguing about phenotype definition, consortium pooling and what rating scales license.
- **Nature** (news feature) — ENIGMA- and ABCD-scale pooling is Nature's own territory, and the "558 MRI measures lose to household income" figure is a strong peg for a field-level reckoning.
- **Undark** — would take the sceptical framing seriously, including the uncomfortable possibility that subdividing symptoms is also an excellent way to generate false positives in small samples.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Neuroimaging — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-02 | **Studies reviewed:** 11
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report
**Digest:** New Scientist Story Ideas, run date 2026-10-02 | **Section:** New Scientist Mind
**Scope:** Abstracts only. Author first names, institutional seniority, and "media check" counts were not independently verifiable and are noted only where they affect a claim about the study.

---

### Study 1: Most children who feel lonely at 10 are still lonely at 14
**PMID:** 42186177 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Persistence overstated — the hook misstates the outcome** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Most children who feel lonely at 10 are still lonely at 14" / "Of the 12% who reported loneliness at baseline, 71.6% reported it again over the next three years" / "seven in ten lonely 10-year-olds are still lonely three years later"
- **Abstract says:** "12% (n = 1,158) reported loneliness at baseline, and 71.6% (n = 829) of those re-experienced loneliness over 3 years." The primary outcome was "prospective loneliness reported from ages 10-14."
- **Problem:** "Re-experienced loneliness over 3 years" means loneliness was reported at some point during follow-up — not that those children were still lonely at the endpoint. The digest body sentence is accurate, but the headline and the pitch angle both convert an "at any point during follow-up" figure into a "still lonely at 14 / three years later" persistence claim. The entire pitch hook rests on the stronger version.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Seven in ten lonely 10-year-olds report loneliness again before 14". Pitch: "seven in ten lonely 10-year-olds reported being lonely again at least once over the next three years."

**Issue B. Unsupported head-to-head comparison of imaging vs environmental predictors** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the slightly deflating result that the brain scans added less than the household income question did"
- **Abstract says:** Environmental and health variables were tested with linear mixed-effects models (|d| = 0.069–0.388 and 0.061–0.390); neuroimaging features were entered into a linear discriminant analysis to distinguish children with and without prospective loneliness. No comparative effect-size statistic is given for imaging.
- **Problem:** The two sets of analyses used different methods and are not reported on a common metric, so the abstract does not support a claim that imaging contributed less than family income. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "the slightly deflating result that the strongest associations were environmental — parental psychopathology, developmental history and family income — while the imaging analysis was a separate classification exercise with no comparable effect size reported."

**Issue C. "Largest prospective test" claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the largest prospective test of that assumption"
- **Abstract says:** Describes a "population-based longitudinal cohort study" of 9,602 ABCD children; makes no priority or size claim.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "this is among the largest prospective tests of that assumption" — or drop the superlative pending verification.

**NS fit:** 7/10 is defensible on cohort size and prospective design, but it is partly earned by the overstated persistence claim. With the corrected framing I would score **6/10**.

---

### Study 2: Brain scans during a failed night's sleep show what insomnia actually looks like
**PMID:** 42458639 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Direct physiological evidence" for hyperarousal overstates the conclusion** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It is direct physiological evidence for the long-argued 'hyperarousal' account of insomnia"
- **Abstract says:** "insomnia was associated with altered nighttime relative cerebral perfusion, including increased activity in self-referential, sensory and affective regions, alongside reduced or dysregulated perfusion in frontal cortex and basal ganglia, suggesting altered arousal regulation, sleep drive and inhibitory control."
- **Problem:** The abstract never uses "hyperarousal" and reports a mixed picture (higher posteriorly, lower frontally) in *relative* perfusion maps from 28 people. "Direct physiological evidence" implies a confirmatory result the design cannot deliver.
- **Suggested fix:** "It is consistent with the long-argued 'hyperarousal' account of insomnia — though with relative, not absolute, perfusion in 28 people, it is suggestive rather than confirmatory."

**Issue B. Sleep state determination described incompletely** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "with polysomnography confirming sleep state"
- **Abstract says:** "Sleep state was determined using self-report and polysomnography."
- **Problem:** Sleep state was classified using both self-report and PSG; the digest presents it as objectively confirmed. This matters because the wider angle pitches the study as a tool for separating paradoxical insomnia from objective short sleep.
- **Suggested fix:** "with sleep state determined from both self-report and polysomnography."

**NS fit:** 6/10 with the small-N limitation explicitly stated is defensible.

### Study 3: Lab experiments missed a brain network that decides where you look
**PMID:** 42772940 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** Title: "The orbitofrontal-anterior temporal network **complements** the attention network for where to look in social situations"; "we could precisely replicate the role of the attention networks in a more natural viewing environment."
- **Problem:** The study explicitly replicates the dorsal and ventral attention networks and adds a complementary network. Nothing is overturned; prior work is described as incomplete. The digest's own body text ("reproduced the classic dorsal and ventral attention networks") contradicts the tag.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Extends/complicates prior research."

**Issue B. "Decides" implies causal control from a similarity analysis** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a brain network that decides where you look"
- **Abstract says:** Activation patterns in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex were found "supporting individual decisions where to look"; the method compared "similarity relationships between eye fixation patterns ... and brain activity patterns."
- **Problem:** A representational-similarity correspondence cannot show the network decides anything; the digest's own caveat says so.
- **Suggested fix:** "Lab experiments missed a brain network tied to where you choose to look."

### Study 4: Impulsive suicidal thoughts leave a different mark on the brain than planned ones
**PMID:** 42710718 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline implies the ideation caused the brain difference** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Impulsive suicidal thoughts **leave a different mark on the brain** than planned ones"
- **Abstract says:** "Hot suicidal ideation was associated with reduced thalamo-pallidal volume compared with no suicidal ideation"; cross-sectional structural MRI in 263 people with MDD.
- **Problem:** "Leave a mark" asserts a direction of effect (thoughts → brain change) that a single-timepoint volumetric association cannot support. The body text and caveats are correctly hedged, so only the headline needs fixing.
- **Suggested fix:** "Impulsive suicidal thoughts are linked to a different brain signature than planned ones."

**Issue B. Single-site description not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "single-site clinical sample of people with MDD"
- **Abstract says:** Reports 263 individuals with MDD; recruitment site(s) not stated (all authors are Poitiers-affiliated).
- **Problem:** Plausible but unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "clinical sample of people with MDD, apparently from a single French centre (confirm with authors)."

Otherwise accurate: the composite (bilateral thalamus, right pallidum), the MADRS-derived subtype, the adjustment set, and the null DLPFC result all match. The pitch's explicit "avoid any suggestion that a scan could identify risk in an individual" is good practice.

### Study 5: Catatonia may be the ancient freeze response jammed on
**PMID:** 42815707 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Systematically cross-referenced" contradicts the review type flagged in Caveats** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The authors **systematically** cross-referenced human neuroimaging of normal threat-induced freezing against imaging of catatonia across its many causes."
- **Abstract says:** "In this critical review, we cross-referenced available neuroimaging studies in human freezing and catatonia studies across etiologies."
- **Problem:** "Systematically" signals systematic-review methodology (prespecified search, screening, selection criteria) that the abstract does not claim; the digest's own caveat correctly calls it a "narrative/critical review."
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors cross-referenced human neuroimaging of normal threat-induced freezing against imaging of catatonia across its many causes in a critical, non-systematic review."

**Issue B. "New mechanism" novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** "It has been suggested that catatonia may be the maladaptive counterpart of the freeze-to-tonic immobility response. While similar brain structures are implicated in both entities, no theory-driven synthesis of neuroimaging evidence has been conducted..."
- **Problem:** The freeze hypothesis pre-dates this paper; what is new is the imaging synthesis and the formalized FAMC model.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** New synthesis of an existing hypothesis."

Note the digest drops "structurally mediated" from the "mechanistically distinct category" list — harmless as an abridgement, but worth restoring if the sentence survives into copy.

### Study 6: Feeling rejected makes you lonely through a specific psychological step — and it looks different in older brains
**PMID:** 42091836 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Causal headline for a cross-sectional mediation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Feeling rejected **makes you lonely** through a specific psychological step"
- **Abstract says:** "withdrawal-related threat sensitivity partially mediated the association between perceived rejection and loneliness"; "These findings provide **preliminary evidence** that withdrawal-related threat sensitivity **may explain the association**..."
- **Problem:** All measures were collected at one timepoint; the digest's own caveat says mediation "cannot establish causal order," which the headline then asserts.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rejection and loneliness are linked by a specific psychological step — and the brain correlates differ by age."

**Issue B. "Not directly" misstates partial mediation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the proposed mechanism: rejection breeds loneliness by ratcheting up a habit of withdrawal, **not directly**"
- **Abstract says:** "withdrawal-related threat sensitivity **partially** mediated the association between perceived rejection and loneliness in both age groups."
- **Problem:** Partial mediation means a direct rejection–loneliness association remains after accounting for threat sensitivity. The pitch tells a writer the opposite — that the route is wholly indirect.
- **Suggested fix:** "the proposed mechanism: part of the link between rejection and loneliness runs through heightened withdrawal-related threat sensitivity, rather than all of it being direct."

**Issue C. Age difference in the pathway overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it looks different in older brains" / "the brain structure associated with the rejection-to-loneliness route was detectable mainly in the young"
- **Abstract says:** "the indirect behavioral association did not differ reliably by age group"; age-sensitive indirect effects were found "in the left precuneus and left planum temporale" only, with the other three regions (left angular gyrus, left subparietal sulcus, right superior temporal sulcus) not described as age-divergent; all imaging analyses were "exploratory."
- **Problem:** Two of five regions showed an age-restricted exploratory effect; the behavioral pathway itself did not differ by age. "Mainly in the young" overgeneralizes.
- **Suggested fix:** "the behavioural pathway was similar in both age groups, but in exploratory analyses two of the five brain regions — left precuneus and left planum temporale — showed the indirect effect only in younger adults."

### Study 7: People who fear punishment are better at waiting for a reward
**PMID:** 42800541 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Better at waiting" frames a preference measure as an ability** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People who fear punishment are **better at** waiting for a reward"
- **Abstract says:** "Behaviorally, punishment sensitivity negatively correlated with delay discounting." Punishment sensitivity is defined as "an individual's tendency to perceive and respond to punishment and other negative outcomes."
- **Problem:** Delay discounting indexes how steeply a person devalues delayed rewards — a preference, measured correlationally — not a demonstrated capacity to wait. "Fear punishment" also narrows the trait definition to fear. Minor, but the headline is the generalization a reader will carry away.
- **Suggested fix:** "People more sensitive to punishment devalue future rewards less."

Everything else checks out: the dmPFC_L GMV association, the dmPFC_L–PCG_R connectivity, the partial mediation with suppressor effect, and the digest's correct note that N is absent from the abstract.

### Study 8: Your sense of numbers runs through the part of the brain that moves your body
**PMID:** 42764054 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts routing from decoding evidence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Your sense of numbers **runs through** the part of the brain that moves your body"
- **Abstract says:** "we revealed significant cross-task decoding between the two semantic modalities within the sensorimotor cortex"; "these findings **suggest** a deep functional coupling between numerical evaluation and motor preparation."
- **Problem:** Decodable information in sensorimotor cortex shows the signal is present there, not that number processing is routed through it; the digest's own caveat says the results "cannot show sensorimotor cortex is necessary."
- **Suggested fix:** "Your sense of numbers shows up in the part of the brain that moves your body."

The behaviour–brain dissociation (SNARC behaviourally only in the implicit parity task; decoding predominantly in the explicit magnitude task) is reported accurately, as is the absence of N from the abstract.

### Study 9: For Māori, the brain is sacred — and MRI practice has no rules for that
**PMID:** 42503436 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline says MRI; participants had EEG** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "For Māori, the brain is sacred — and **MRI** practice has no rules for that"
- **Abstract says:** "Semi-structured uiuinga (interviews) with three Māori men ... who had previously participated in an **electroencephalography** session"; "there are currently no national-level guidelines for conducting **neuroimaging** in Aotearoa."
- **Problem:** The participants' lived experience was of EEG, and the guideline gap described is for neuroimaging generally. Naming MRI in the headline attributes experience the participants did not report — and the pitch's own imagery ("gelling and electrode-capping the head") is EEG, not MRI.
- **Suggested fix:** "For Māori, the brain is sacred — and neuroimaging practice has no rules for that."

**Issue B. Dataset-representation inference goes beyond the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "assumptions that affect who consents to be scanned, and therefore who is represented in brain datasets"
- **Abstract says:** Addresses culturally safe care, relational engagement, shared decision-making and whānau confidence; says nothing about recruitment rates or dataset composition.
- **Problem:** A reasonable hypothesis, but presented as a finding of this study. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "assumptions that researchers in this area argue may shape who feels able to take part — a link this study does not itself measure."

**NS fit:** 5/10 for a three-participant qualitative study is appropriately cautious, and the score note already explains why.

### Study 11: Depressed people who are sleepy by day lose pleasure in physical things
**PMID:** 42746369 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Matched" implies a design feature the abstract does not report** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The two groups were **matched** on depression and anxiety severity *and* on objective sleep parameters"
- **Abstract says:** "The two groups were comparable for demographic and clinical characteristics, with no differences in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) or Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) scores or polysomnographic parameters."
- **Problem:** Groups were observed to be comparable, not matched by design — a distinction that matters because the "identical sleep studies" pitch leans on it.
- **Suggested fix:** "The two groups did not differ on depression or anxiety severity, or on polysomnographic sleep parameters."

**Issue B. "Anticipatory" anhedonia vs the instrument used** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "higher specifically on physical anhedonia — not social or **anticipatory** anhedonia"
- **Abstract says:** "The DS group scored higher on the RPAS, while social and **temporal** anhedonia did not differ between groups" (TEPS = Temporal Experience of Pleasure Scale, which covers anticipatory *and* consummatory pleasure).
- **Problem:** "Anticipatory" names only half of what the TEPS measures.
- **Suggested fix:** "not social or temporal (anticipatory and consummatory) anhedonia."

**Issue C. Headline implies a change over time** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Depressed people who are sleepy by day **lose** pleasure in physical things"
- **Abstract says:** Cross-sectional design; "MDD patients with DS exhibit more severe physical anhedonia."
- **Problem:** "Lose" describes a trajectory; the study measured a between-group difference at one timepoint. The caveats correctly flag cross-sectionality.
- **Suggested fix:** "Depressed people who are sleepy by day report less pleasure in physical things."

**NS fit:** 4/10 is appropriately low for 22 vs 45 with a cross-sectional mediation.
